Practise explaining the mechanisms in [the lecture](lec.qmd), then use the
[quiz](quiz.qmd) for a shorter self-check. G questions cover the core outcomes;
VG questions ask you to predict, interpret data or design a test. Try each answer
before opening the model answer.

## G-level questions

**1.** Draw a mitochondrion and label its outer membrane, intermembrane space,
inner membrane, cristae and matrix. Place the TCA cycle, respiratory chain,
ATP synthase head and cytochrome c. Why do the two membranes have different
permeabilities? `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
The **matrix** lies inside the inner membrane and contains most TCA-cycle enzymes
(succinate dehydrogenase is complex II in the inner membrane). The respiratory
complexes and ATP synthase sit in the **inner membrane**, including its cristae;
the synthase head faces the matrix. **Cytochrome c** carries electrons along the
intermembrane-space side of the inner membrane. The **outer membrane** contains
porins that pass small solutes. The inner membrane requires specific carriers and
has low proton permeability, so it can store an **electrochemical H⁺ gradient**.
Cristae increase the area available for energy conversion.
:::

---

**2.** Explain how electrons from NADH reach oxygen, which complexes pump H⁺,
and how the resulting gradient drives ATP synthesis. Why does succinate-linked
entry through complex II yield less ATP per electron pair? `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Electrons pass **I → ubiquinone (Q) → III → cytochrome c → IV → O₂**, reducing
oxygen to water. Complexes **I, III and IV** move H⁺ from matrix to intermembrane
space: about **10 H⁺ per NADH**. The matrix becomes negative and alkaline; both
components favour H⁺ return. Return through ATP synthase turns its c-ring and
central stalk. The fixed β catalytic sites change conformation to bind ADP and
phosphate, form ATP and release it. Electron transport and ATP synthesis are
coupled through the gradient (**chemiosmosis**). Complex II transfers electrons
from succinate to Q without pumping H⁺, bypassing I: about **6 H⁺** are pumped per
electron pair instead of 10.
:::

---

**3.** The matrix is 160 mV negative relative to the intermembrane space and
0.5 pH unit more alkaline. Estimate the magnitude of the proton-motive force
at 37 °C, taking 61.5 mV per pH unit. What happens if H⁺ can freely cross the
inner membrane? `[ELO 2, ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Both electrical and chemical components favour H⁺ entry, so their magnitudes add:
**160 + 0.5 × 61.5 ≈ 191 mV**. This is the magnitude; Δψ is negative when defined
as matrix minus intermembrane-space potential. H⁺ leakage dissipates the stored
energy. Electron transport can continue, and often accelerates, but less of its
energy is captured in ATP and more becomes heat. A gradient is energy stored
across the membrane, not a large reservoir of free protons.
:::

---

**4.** How does ATP made in the matrix become available in the cytosol? Explain
why the ADP/ATP carrier depends on the membrane potential and why ATP synthesis
also needs phosphate transport. `[ELO 2, ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
The inner membrane does not freely pass ATP or ADP. The **ADP/ATP antiporter**
exports ATP⁴⁻ in exchange for ADP³⁻, moving one net negative charge out of the
negative matrix: the voltage favours export. The **phosphate carrier** imports
phosphate with H⁺ (equivalently, phosphate/OH⁻ exchange). These carriers spend
part of the proton-motive force, adding roughly one proton-equivalent to the
cost per ATP delivered. Porins allow the nucleotides to cross the outer membrane.
The mammalian synthase itself uses **8/3 H⁺ per ATP**; delivery and proton leaks
help explain why practical ATP yields are lower than the ideal rotor ratio.
:::

---

**5.** What does human mtDNA encode? Why do mitochondria still need protein
import? Distinguish maternal inheritance of mtDNA from inheritance of a
mitochondrial disease caused by a nuclear gene. `[ELO 4, ELO 5, ELO 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Human mtDNA has **37 genes: 13 proteins, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs**. The 13 proteins
are core subunits of complexes I, III, IV and ATP synthase; complex II is entirely
nuclear encoded. Most mitochondrial proteins are encoded in the nucleus, made
on cytosolic ribosomes and imported, often through **TOM/TIM**. Mitochondrial DNA
is normally inherited from the egg, so fathers do not transmit mtDNA variants.
Nuclear genes follow their own Mendelian inheritance patterns and can be
transmitted by either parent. A mitochondrial disease is therefore **not
necessarily maternally inherited**.
:::

---

**6.** Explain heteroplasmy, the threshold effect and the mitochondrial genetic
bottleneck. Why can siblings have different symptoms, and why are brain,
heart and skeletal muscle often affected? `[ELO 5, ELO 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
**Heteroplasmy** means that different mtDNA variants coexist in a cell or person,
here normal and disease-causing copies. During egg development, sampling and
amplification of mtDNA produce eggs with different mutant fractions (the
**bottleneck**). Fractions can also differ between tissues. Dysfunction becomes
apparent when the remaining capacity cannot meet tissue needs: the **threshold**
depends on the variant and tissue, not one universal percentage. Siblings can
therefore inherit different mutant loads and have different disease severity;
maternal heteroplasmy does not mean that every child must be affected. High
energy demand makes brain, heart and muscle particularly vulnerable.
:::

---

**7.** Compare mitochondrial fission and fusion. How do they cooperate with
mitophagy to maintain the network? `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
**Fission**, involving DRP1, divides tubules; **fusion** joins outer membranes
through mitofusins and inner membranes through OPA1. Fusion mixes contents and
can complement local defects. Fission helps segregate damaged regions and
provides mitochondria for distribution during cell division. Selected damaged
mitochondria can be enclosed by autophagosomes and degraded in lysosomes
(**mitophagy**). Fragmentation alone does not prove that mitophagy or cell death
has occurred: removal must be measured separately.
:::

---

**8.** Give two roles of mitochondria beyond ATP production. Explain why both
Ca²⁺ uptake and ROS can be useful at moderate levels and harmful in excess.
What changes when cytochrome c reaches the cytosol? `[ELO 5, ELO 8]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
At **ER–mitochondria contacts**, released Ca²⁺ enters the matrix through the
mitochondrial calcium uniporter, driven by the negative matrix potential. This
shapes Ca²⁺ signals and activates metabolic enzymes. Ca²⁺ overload can promote
permeability transition and injury. Electron leakage makes **ROS**: controlled
levels participate in signalling, whereas excessive ROS damage lipids, proteins
and DNA. Cytochrome c normally transfers electrons between III and IV. After
**BAX/BAK** permeabilise the outer membrane, cytosolic cytochrome c binds APAF1,
helping assemble the apoptosome and activate caspase-9 and executioner caspases.
Location changes its effect.
:::

---

**9.** Compare chemiosmosis in mitochondria and chloroplasts. Which membrane
holds the gradient, which side accumulates H⁺, and where does the ATP synthase
head face? `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Mitochondria use the **inner membrane**: H⁺ are pumped from the matrix into the
intermembrane space and return to the matrix-facing synthase head. Chloroplasts
use the **thylakoid membrane**: light-driven electron transport accumulates H⁺
in the thylakoid lumen; H⁺ return to the **stroma**, where ATP is made. The envelope
around a chloroplast is not the membrane across which photosynthetic ATP
synthesis is coupled. Both use an electrochemical gradient and a rotary synthase.
:::

## VG-level questions

**10. [VG]** A stress test gives the following representative oxygen consumption
rates from equal numbers of viable cells. Assume each phase has reached a stable
rate and FCCP has been optimised. Calculate basal mitochondrial respiration,
ATP-linked respiration, proton leak, maximal respiration, spare capacity and
coupling efficiency. Is maximal respiration also maximal ATP production?
`[ELO 1, ELO 5]`

| Phase | OCR (pmol O₂/min) |
|---|---:|
| Before drugs | 120 |
| After oligomycin | 40 |
| After FCCP | 200 |
| After rotenone + antimycin A | 20 |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Non-mitochondrial OCR is **20**. Subtract it where appropriate:

- Basal mitochondrial respiration: 120 − 20 = **100 pmol O₂/min**.
- ATP-linked respiration: 120 − 40 = **80 pmol O₂/min**.
- Proton leak: 40 − 20 = **20 pmol O₂/min**.
- Maximal respiration: 200 − 20 = **180 pmol O₂/min**.
- Spare capacity: 180 − 100 = **80 pmol O₂/min**.
- Coupling efficiency: 80/100 = **80 %**.

FCCP allows proton return independently of ATP synthase, and oligomycin is still
present. Therefore the high OCR is **not high mitochondrial ATP production**.
OCR measures oxygen use; converting it into ATP production needs additional
assumptions. In real experiments use replicates, normalise to cell number or
protein, and optimise drug concentrations.
:::

---

**11. [VG]** Predict the immediate effects of oligomycin, an uncoupler and
cyanide on electron flow, proton-motive force and mitochondrial ATP synthesis
in oxygenated cells supplied with fuel. Why can FCCP increase OCR after
oligomycin but not after cyanide? What could maintain some cellular ATP?
`[ELO 5, ELO 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
| Treatment | Electron flow / mitochondrial OCR | Proton-motive force | ATP synthesis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Oligomycin | Falls as the gradient opposes further pumping | Initially rises | Blocked at synthase |
| Uncoupler | Usually rises if respiratory capacity and fuel remain | Falls | Falls strongly |
| Cyanide | Falls: complex IV cannot reduce O₂ | Decays as H⁺ return without replenishment | Falls as the gradient is lost |

FCCP bypasses the blocked proton return pathway after oligomycin: pumping and
electron flow resume through an intact chain. It cannot bypass **blocked electron
transfer** at IV. The same distinction explains heat production by DNP.
**Glycolysis** can maintain some ATP; a fall in mitochondrial ATP production does
not mean all cellular ATP instantly becomes zero. Severe uncoupling eventually
impairs cellular function, so the early OCR prediction need not hold indefinitely.
:::

---

**12. [VG]** Design a test of the claim that a proton gradient is sufficient to
couple an unrelated proton pump to ATP synthesis. Include controls. Then explain
why mitochondrial donation can reduce the risk of mtDNA disease but cannot
correct a pathogenic nuclear allele. `[ELO 1, ELO 5, ELO 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}
Reconstitute a light-driven H⁺ pump and ATP synthase into sealed lipid vesicles,
with orientations that let the pump create a gradient driving H⁺ through the
synthase. Supply ADP and phosphate on the synthase-head side. Compare **light vs
dark**, vesicles missing either protein, and complete vesicles with an **uncoupler**.
Measure ATP accumulation and check the gradient independently with a suitable
probe. ATP should accumulate when both proteins and light generate a usable
gradient, and should fall when that gradient is dissipated. The controls exclude
ATP contamination and demonstrate that shared electron-transfer machinery is
unnecessary.

Donation transfers the parents' nuclear material to donor cytoplasm containing
mostly donor mtDNA. It reduces transmission of maternal mutant mtDNA, although
some may be carried over. A **nuclear allele moves with the nuclear material**,
so donation does not remove it. This is a change of cellular compartment/genome
source, not repair of the mutation.
:::

## Explore {#explore}

**Demo: mito stress test.** Predict the trace, then measure a simulated well and
watch the proton circuit. It starts at **1× assay time**: one point per six
minutes, three points per phase. Select **240×** for a quick run (about 4.5 seconds
per phase). The particles and rotor are slowed illustrations; the values are
from a qualitative model, not patient data. Drug additions persist until you
start a new well. The model assumes adequate fuel, an optimised FCCP dose and a
fixed non-mitochondrial OCR; it omits glycolytic ATP and long-term cell responses.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="mitostress"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/mitostress.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Run **Healthy cell**. After the basal phase, inject **oligomycin → FCCP →
rotenone + antimycin A**, waiting for each phase to finish. Explain the change in
OCR and Δp after every injection. `[ELO 5]`

**E2.** Use the completed trace to calculate ATP-linked respiration and spare
capacity yourself. Compare your calculations with the table. Why do you subtract
the final residual OCR? `[ELO 1, ELO 5]`

**E3. [VG]** Predict, then compare **Complex I defect** with Healthy cell at the
same ATP demand. Which results suggest reduced respiratory capacity? Does OCR
alone prove a defect in complex I? `[ELO 1, ELO 5, ELO 9]`

**E4. [VG]** Start a new well and inject **FCCP before oligomycin**, then finish
with rotenone + antimycin A. Which quantities can you still estimate, and which
are lost? Repeat with rotenone + antimycin A first. `[ELO 1, ELO 5]`

**E5. [VG]** Increase **ATP demand** and repeat the standard sequence in Healthy
cell. Predict basal respiration and spare capacity. Compare the high-concentration
metformin preset: what conclusion about therapeutic metformin can this model
support? `[ELO 5, ELO 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** Oligomycin closes the ATP synthase proton route: Δp rises, pumping faces
more back-pressure, and OCR falls. FCCP opens a proton bypass: Δp falls and OCR
rises even though the synthase is still blocked. Rotenone + antimycin A stop
chain flux: only non-mitochondrial OCR remains, and the gradient decays.

**E2.** ATP-linked = last basal OCR − lowest oligomycin OCR; maximal = highest
FCCP OCR − final residual; basal mitochondrial = last basal OCR − residual;
spare = maximal − basal mitochondrial. The residual comes from oxygen-consuming
processes outside the respiratory chain. Seeded measurement noise causes small
variation, so calculate from your well rather than expecting exact fixed values.

**E3.** The preset lowers chain capacity: maximal and spare respiration fall,
and ATP production is harder to sustain. Similar traces can arise from other
respiratory defects, fuel limitation or fewer viable cells. Check cell number,
viability and mitochondrial abundance; use substrate-specific or biochemical
tests to locate the defect. The model assumes a complex I defect; it does not
diagnose one from the trace.

**E4.** FCCP before oligomycin preserves an uncoupled maximum and the final
residual, but loses the coupled oligomycin comparison: **ATP-linked respiration,
proton leak and coupling efficiency cannot be recovered** by the standard method.
Rotenone + antimycin A first stop electron flow, so subsequent injections cannot
reveal ATP-linked or maximal respiratory capacity. Basal and residual OCR remain
available.

**E5.** Higher ATP demand increases proton return through synthase and raises
basal OCR; with the same chain maximum, spare capacity falls. The metformin preset
illustrates what partial respiratory-chain inhibition *could* do. Its parameters
are chosen, not measured at therapeutic exposure; it cannot establish metformin's
clinical mechanism or predict a patient's response.
:::

The calculation conventions follow the
[Agilent assay guide](https://www.agilent.com/cs/library/usermanuals/public/XF_Cell_Mito_Stress_Test_Kit_User_Guide.pdf).
